message.content:
**Freezing point of water at 10 kPa**

| Pressure | Freezing (melting) point of water |
|----------|-----------------------------------|
| 10 kPa   | **≈ –2.2 °C** |

---

### Why it’s lower than 0 °C

Water’s phase diagram shows that the solid–liquid equilibrium line (the melting curve) slopes downward as pressure decreases.  
- At the standard atmospheric pressure (≈ 101.3 kPa) the melting point is 0 °C.  
- At 10 kPa (about 0.1 atm) the equilibrium temperature drops to roughly –2.2 °C.

This depression is due to the fact that ice has a lower density than liquid water; reducing the pressure favors the less‑dense phase (ice), so it can form at a slightly lower temperature.

---

### Quick check with the Clausius–Clapeyron relation

The Clausius–Clapeyron equation for the solid–liquid boundary can be approximated as:

\[
\frac{dT}{dP} \approx \frac{T\,\Delta V}{\Delta H_{\text{fus}}}
\]

Using typical values for water (\(\Delta H_{\text{fus}} \approx 6.01 \times 10^3\) J mol⁻¹, \(\Delta V \approx 1.9 \times 10^{-5}\) m³ mol⁻¹ at 0 °C) gives a slope of about –0.007 °C kPa⁻¹ near 1 atm. Integrating from 101.3 kPa down to 10 kPa yields a temperature drop of roughly –2 °C, consistent with the tabulated value.

---

### Bottom line

At a pressure of **10 kPa**, water freezes (melts) at approximately **–2.2 °C**.
